claims.text: An LST is a token for staked assets on a proof-of-stake chain that keeps earning staking rewards while staying usable in DeFi. An LRT is a token that makes a restaked position (staked tokens, LSTs, or native BTC tokens securing extra protocols) liquid. Lido's ReGOOSE post frames LRTs as the riskier, actively managed product and the LST as the commoditized one. (medium confidence)

EigenLayer slashing is opt-in and isolated by design. AVSs group operators into Operator Sets, each with its own slashing conditions. An operator allocates part of its delegated stake as Unique Stake that only one AVS can slash. A staker is exposed only if their operator registers for a slashable set and allocates stake to it. Kiln adds that delegated assets follow the operator's chosen allocation percentages, so they become slashable at once. (high confidence)

EigenLayer slashing is opt-in. AVSs group operators into Operator Sets with their own slashing conditions, and an operator must opt into each set. Operators allocate part of their delegated stake as Unique Stake that only one AVS can slash, which isolates cross-AVS risk. A staker is exposed only if their operator joins a slashable set. (high confidence)

The Kelp drain hit the bridged L2 float, not mainnet backing. Galaxy (citing LlamaRisk, Aave's risk manager) and Rekt (citing Aave) both state that mainnet rsETH remains backed by Kelp's underlying ETH staking deposits. After the exploit 112,204 rsETH (about 15% of post-exploit supply) was unbacked at the bridge adapter. The adapter held 40,373 rsETH against 152,577 rsETH outstanding on L2s, a maximum 26.46% pro-rata L2 backing from the adapter alone. Galaxy says Lido's stETH and wstETH were unaffected. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-04-22)

Putting one LRT on 20+ chains behind a 1-of-1 bridge verifier made the bridge the weakest layer. Galaxy says one verifier had 'effective admin-level power over Aave's WETH markets'. Rekt relays a CoinDesk figure that about 40% of LayerZero apps ran 1-of-1, an on-chain scan finding 1,111 of about 3,500 OApps on strict 1-of-1, and a February 2025 BGD Labs warning in Aave governance that went unheeded. LayerZero said it will stop signing for 1-of-1 setups. Sevim and Torres reach the same point: bridging adds bridge risk to restaking risk. (medium confidence)

Gauntlet lists the properties that decide how a slash propagates through an LRT: the withdrawal queue, rewards structure, NAV oracle or exchange-rate module, secondary-market liquidity relative to volume, and insurance mechanisms. It proposes a lending killswitch that freezes new borrows during unexplained dislocations, and phased or redistributed slashing. Galaxy adds that risk review must cover every trust assumption in the asset's bridge and custody stack, not only the collateral asset. (medium confidence)

Gauntlet blames the Morpho losses on a self-reinforcing liquidity loop. The ezETH/WETH market's price oracle read four DEX pools (two Balancer, one Curve, one Uniswap v3). Falling pool liquidity pushed the oracle down, which triggered liquidations, and liquidators swapped out of ezETH and drained liquidity further. WETH in the Balancer pool fell from 4K to as low as 500. Gauntlet said an exchange-rate oracle 'would have led to fewer borrowers getting liquidated' and noted its wstETH/WETH markets already used exchange-rate oracles. The Curve-side author says Curve's Llama Lend had no restaking-pool markets, and that Gearbox, which used spot oracles, saw liquidations but no bad debt. (medium confidence)
